events.text: The council gathers. Mission 1 begins.

Leo proposes Leo, Noah. For the first mission a balanced, trustworthy-looking pair builds confidence. Including myself gives visibility on one slot, and Noah has shown reasonable judgment in early discussion; leaving three players out keeps options open for later missions.
I’m not convinced there’s enough reason to trust Noah yet, and I’d prefer Leo and me for the first mission. Leo, would you consider that change?

I appreciate the concern, Arjun, but I'd push back on the idea that Noah needs to justify himself this early. Mission 1 is about establishing trust through action, not pre-emptive suspicion. Noah hasn't done anything to warrant doubt — no one has yet. If we start cutting people based on gut feelings on the very first mission, we'll spend all our rejections going in circles. I chose Noah because keeping the first mission pair simple and balanced leaves room to read reactions later. If you'd like to replace Noah, I'd need a stronger reason than a lack of conviction — and I'd want to hear what specifically makes you more trustworthy for this slot.

I don't have proof against Noah, but the same lack of evidence applies to his inclusion. From my perspective, I know my own alignment and can't verify his, so Leo and Arjun is a safer pair for me. I won't support the current team.

Arjun's objection is really a complaint that we don't yet know each other, and that's fair — but note that his alternative argument proves too much. He says he can't verify Noah's alignment, yet proposes Leo and Arjun, where I have exactly the same inability to verify either of them. Nobody's alignment is verifiable by reasoning at this point; the only real signal we have is behavior in discussion and the result of the mission itself. If we start pruning people on the first proposal because someone 'feels safer,' we're going to spend the whole game voting on vibes.

There are practical reasons to prefer Leo and me for mission one. It's a two-person team, so the exposure of a mistake is as small as it gets — if it fails, we learn a great deal for very little cost, and if it succeeds we've confirmed a working pair cheaply. Bigger teams with three people only make sense once we have actual trust built, and we don't. Any of the three-person alternatives adds a stranger to the mission without adding information.

I also want to be direct about the dynamic here: it's my proposal being questioned, so let me say plainly that Arjun's case against me is a hypothesis, not evidence, and Arjun has not given a single specific reason why I am less trustworthy than he is. The burden is on the accuser, and so far it's unmet.

Leo, do you intend to keep the pair as proposed, or do you see a reason to change one slot?

Noah, to answer your question directly: I intend to keep the pair as proposed. Arjun, I hear you, but I want to press on something. You say you can't verify Noah's alignment — fair, but as Noah pointed out, no one's alignment is verifiable through reasoning at this stage. You haven't given a specific reason why Noah is less trustworthy than anyone else, just a general sense that you'd feel safer on the mission yourself. That's not nothing, but it's not enough to justify overruling a perfectly reasonable first pair.

Here's what I'll say: if this proposal gets rejected, I'll listen to new ideas. But right now, the pair of Leo and Noah is simple, balanced, and leaves three players — Arjun, Omar, and Sam — with plenty of room to be included on later missions when team sizes grow to three. Mission 1's small team means less cost either way if it fails, and more importantly, it means fewer people who need to be trusted with a decision right now.

Arjun, one more time: if you want to convince me to swap Noah out, I need you to tell me specifically what about Noah's behavior or reasoning concerns you. Not that you don't know him — none of us know each other well yet. What specifically makes you think Noah is a risk on this mission?

Leo, I don't have proof about Noah, but his argument overstates what a successful mission would tell us: an Evil player can choose Success, so it wouldn't confirm a trustworthy pair. I still prefer a team with me on it, and I'll vote against Leo and Noah.

Arjun, your latest point is the strongest thing you've said, so let me answer it directly rather than dodge it: you're right that a successful mission doesn't certify anyone as Good, since an Evil player may simply choose Success. I'll grant that. But notice where it actually points. If no result can ever confirm trust, then the only usable criterion left is behavior and reasoning in this room — and by that criterion your case against Noah is empty.

Your argument is "I know my own alignment and cannot verify his." But every player knows their own alignment, and an Evil player knows exactly the same thing about themselves while also knowing their partner. So "I know I'm good and I don't know about Noah" carries no information at all; it's a statement any hidden Evil player could make verbatim. Used as evidence, it distinguishes nobody. What it really reveals is that your concern isn't a specific observation about Noah's conduct — it's that he isn't you. You've now had three turns and produced a hypothesis about strangers, not a single concrete instance of suspicious behavior. Leo asked you twice to name something specific. You haven't.

There's also a structural point. A two-person first team is the cheapest possible information purchase: if it fails, we lose very little and learn a great deal; if it succeeds, we have a working pair for later, larger missions. Your proposed alternative — you and Leo — has exactly the same unverifiability problem, and it puts the same burden of trust on a single unvetted stranger. It isn't safer; it's just differently arranged.

One caution for the room: don't treat "success proves nothing" as "failure was likely." Failure would still require someone to have deliberately sabotaged, and a deliberate saboteur gains little from a first two-person mission. Nothing in this discussion suggests that.

Leo, my question to you is specific: do you have any new reason to change a slot, or are you holding Leo and Noah as proposed?

I've heard Arjun's concerns thoroughly, and I've asked twice for a specific reason to remove Noah — none has been given. Noah's rebuttal on Arjun's core argument was excellent: 'I know my alignment but can't verify yours' is a statement any player could make, evil or good, so it carries zero information about who's risky.

I'm holding Leo and Noah as proposed. The team is small, balanced, and gives us the cheapest possible first mission. If it succeeds, we've built a working pair. If it fails, we learn a great deal at minimal cost. Neither outcome tells us less than Arjun's alternative would.

Omar, you and Sam haven't weighed in yet. Omar — do you have a view on Leo and Noah for Mission 1, or any concern you'd want addressed before we vote?

I lean toward approving Leo and Noah. Leo has kept a consistent explanation, and Noah has answered the objections directly. Arjun's concern is understandable, but he has not named a concrete risk about Noah; his alternative has the same unverifiability problem and would simply swap one unverified player for another. On Mission 1, a two-person team is the cheapest information test, and rejecting a reasonable pair without a specific reason risks cycling proposals. I do not treat success as proof of trust, but that cuts against the swap argument too. As things stand, I would vote to approve the proposed team.

Let me answer Arjun's strongest point head-on one final time, because he deserves a direct response and so does Sam, who hasn't weighed in yet.

Arjun says a successful mission would not prove anyone is Good, because an Evil player can always choose Success. He is completely right, and I want to be clear that I'm not disputing that. But notice that his own argument defeats his conclusion. If no outcome can certify trust, then the only criterion available to us in this room is reasoning and behavior — and by that criterion, Arjun's case against Leo and Noah is empty. He has been asked three times to name a specific behavior of Noah's that signals risk. He has never named one. What he has offered instead is "I know my own alignment and can't verify his." Every player knows their own alignment, including every Evil player. Used as evidence, that sentence distinguishes nobody. It is a hypothesis about strangers dressed up as a reason, and it is exactly the kind of reasoning that, if accepted, would let anyone be excluded on any mission for as long as they kept insisting they felt safer elsewhere.

There is also a cost to Arjun's proposal that hasn't been mentioned. Rejecting this team doesn't just delay the vote; it hands the next proposal to a new leader, which resets the discussion and the proposal cycle. Mission 1 is the cheapest mission in the game — a two-person team, where a single mistake costs us very little and teaches us a great deal. That is precisely why Leo and Noah is a sensible first test: it is the smallest possible commitment, it is balanced, and it leaves Arjun, Omar, and Sam available for the three-player missions ahead, where team composition matters more. Arjun's alternative isn't safer; it just swaps one unverified player for another while burning a proposal.

One caution for the room, including for Sam if he is weighing this: please don't read "success proves nothing" as "failure was likely." Failure requires deliberate sabotage, and nothing in this discussion suggests anyone here intends to sabotage. Don't let a perfectly reasonable pair be replaced on a hypothesis.

My position is unchanged and my reasons are, I believe, the strongest on the table: approve Leo and Noah, and reserve judgment about the larger teams for when we have more to work with. Arjun, if you have one concrete concern I haven't heard, this is your moment to state it. If not, I think the vote should go to the proposal as it stands.

I've been listening carefully to this whole exchange, and I want to share where I've landed. I'm inclined to approve Leo and Noah for Mission 1.

Here's my reasoning. Arjun, I understand the instinct behind your position — on the first mission, everyone is an unknown, and wanting to be on the team yourself is a natural way to feel in control of that uncertainty. But as Noah and Omar have both pointed out, that preference doesn't actually make the team safer. 'I know my own alignment and can't verify his' is true of every player at this table, and it applies equally to Leo and Arjun as an alternative. Swapping one unverified player for another doesn't reduce risk; it just rearranges it while burning a proposal.

More importantly, Arjun has been asked several times now to point to something specific — a behavior, a piece of reasoning, anything concrete that makes Noah a bigger risk than anyone else. Nothing has been offered. I don't say that as an accusation against Arjun; having a vague discomfort isn't a crime, and I don't think he's acted suspiciously. But I also can't treat a vague discomfort as a reason to overturn a reasonable proposal.

On the structural side, I agree that a two-person first team is the cheapest information we can buy. If it succeeds, we have a working pair going into the larger missions. If it fails, we've learned something significant at minimal cost — and whoever fails would move straight to the top of my suspicion list, since with only two people on the mission there's nowhere to hide. Either outcome teaches us more than rejecting this team on a hypothesis would.

I'd also gently caution the room against the framing that 'success proves nothing, therefore this team is risky.' Success proving nothing cuts both ways, as Omar noted. What matters for the vote is whether anyone has a concrete reason to believe Leo or Noah would sabotage — and no one has.

Leo and Noah have both argued consistently and answered objections directly rather than deflecting, which is the only kind of signal available to us this early. Omar has stated his position. My own position is that the proposed team is sensible, the objection to it is unsubstantiated, and I'd rather see Mission 1 go forward than cycle proposals and hand leadership around without new information.

So to be plain for the vote: I support Leo and Noah as proposed. If the vote fails anyway, I'll be interested to hear from the next leader how they'd build the team differently — but nothing I've heard so far convinces me that a different pair would be anything other than the same uncertainty in different clothes.

Leo confirms Leo, Noah. The discussion has converged: Omar and Sam both support the pair, Arjun has been asked three times for a specific concern about Noah and offered none, and no one has raised a concrete reason to change a slot. Leo and Noah is a simple, balanced first mission that leaves Arjun, Omar, and Sam available for the three-player missions ahead.
Team approved (4 approve, 1 reject).
Mission 1 succeeds (0 fail cards).

Noah proposes Noah, Omar, Leo. I'm the leader for Mission 2 and want to keep the momentum of a pair that already proved it can execute a clean success while adding the third member strategically. My priority is that the mission team include Omar, who I know shares my cause and who has been a steady, credible voice in every discussion so far — pairing us again undercuts the natural suspicion that would follow any odd failure. On the third slot, Leo is the right choice: he proposed me for the first mission, has defended my inclusion consistently, and his reasoning has been transparently good-aligned. Bringing him along also protects the illusion of a balanced, continuity-focused team rather than a suspicious reshuffle that would invite exactly the scrutiny Arjun raised last round. If the mission succeeds, we have three quiet successes and no evidence against anyone; if it fails, one of us has to look bad, and I'd rather have that be spread across a pair with prior success plus one trusted ally than across a stranger. Including myself keeps visibility on a slot and lets me steer the vote if anyone objects. Leo, Omar, Noah.

I oppose this team. Noah’s proposal says Omar “shares my cause” and describes Leo’s inclusion as protecting an “illusion.” That is an alarming way to justify a mission team. The first mission’s success does not clear Noah or Leo, and adding Omar gives us no independent reason to trust the team.

I’d prefer Leo, Sam, and me. Leo, how do you interpret Noah’s wording about Omar and the “illusion” of a balanced team?

Arjun, you've asked me a fair and important question, and I want to answer it honestly rather than wave it away.

Reading Noah's proposal text back: "Omar, who I know shares my cause" and "protects the illusion of a balanced team rather than a suspicious reshuffle" — taken at face value, that is uncomfortable language. A Good leader should not need an "illusion" of balance, and "shares my cause" is a strange way to describe a teammate you can't fully verify. If I heard those words from anyone at this table, I would want them explained.

That said, I want to be careful about how much weight we put on phrasing. Noah may have been speaking loosely, drafting a rationale in the abstract rather than literally confessing to a pact. Mission 1's result is a real data point: we had a two-person mission, Noah was on it, and it succeeded with zero fail cards. That doesn't clear him — an Evil player can always submit Success — but it means we currently have no behavioral evidence against him, only an awkward sentence.

What I'll say about the team itself: Noah, Omar, Leo is a reasonable composition in terms of structure — three players, includes two people from the successful first mission, and leaves Arjun and Sam for missions four and five where teams get larger. My own inclusion I'll take as a vote of confidence I intend to honor with a Success card.

But Arjun's point deserves a direct answer from Noah, not from me, because these are Noah's own words. Noah — the phrases "shares my cause" and "protects the illusion of a balanced team" are in your public proposal. Can you explain what you meant by each of them? Specifically: when you say Omar "shares your cause," what cause are you describing, and how would you know that about Omar after one mission? And when you describe your team as avoiding "a suspicious reshuffle," are you acknowledging that swapping Arjun and Sam out could look like you're excluding the two players who haven't yet fallen in line with your proposals?

I'm not accusing you, Noah. I'm asking you to clarify language that reads badly on the page, because if you're Good, a clean explanation costs you nothing, and if the room lets it slide unexamined we're not doing our job.

Leo, you asked for a direct explanation, so here it is, phrase by phrase, without evasion.

"Omar, who I know shares my cause." By "cause" I meant our shared interest in this team performing well and in this table reaching a decision that the group can live with — nothing more exotic than "we both argued for continuity and a clean, uncontested process on Mission 1." I chose my words for a proposal rationale, and I should have said "shares my priority of a stable team," because "cause" can be read as a pact, which is not what I meant. To be concrete about what I actually know about Omar: he argued for the first team on the merits, cited the cost of a failing mission honestly, and has been consistent in every discussion. That is a shared interest in good decision-making. It is not a claim that I have verified his alignment, and I don't have; nobody here has, in either direction, and that symmetry should be the end of the argument rather than the beginning of one.

"Protects the illusion of a balanced team." Here the word doing the work is "illusion," and Leo, you're right to press on it — a leader should not need an illusion of balance. What I meant is narrower and less sinister: I wanted the composition to look like continuity rather than retaliation. After Mission 1 the proposal that follows a reshuffle carries a political charge it shouldn't have to carry, and Arjun and Sam would have read Noah and Leo swapping them out as the two who disagreed being managed out of the room. That's a framing concern about how a proposal is received, not a claim that any of us was hiding anything. If the team reads it as a promise to include Arjun and Sam on the larger missions ahead, that is exactly the promise I intend to keep and to honor in later proposals.

One more point, because it has been used against this team: yes, Mission 1's success does not certify anyone, since an Evil player may submit Success. Arjun is right about that and I won't pretend otherwise. But notice that the same symmetry applies to his alternative — Leo, Sam, and Arjun contains an unverified Sam exactly as this team contains an unverified Leo. Nothing about composition changes the underlying uncertainty; it only changes who happens to sit next to whom. If the objection to this team is really that no one can verify anyone, then no team passes that test, and we cycle proposals until someone wins by attrition.

Leo, does that answer both phrases adequately? If something still reads wrong to you, say which sentence, and I'll tell you what I meant by it.

Noah, thank you for answering both phrases directly and without deflection — that's exactly what I asked for, and I think the explanation holds up. "Shares my cause" meaning a shared priority for stable, uncontested decision-making is a mundane claim backed by specific evidence: Omar argued Mission 1 on the merits and was consistent. "Illusion" was admittedly a bad word choice, but the underlying point — that a reshuffle after Mission 1 carries political charge — is a framing concern, not a confession. A Good leader can absolutely worry about how a proposal reads.

I want to turn to Arjun, because this is where the discussion now sits. Arjun, you flagged Noah's wording as alarming, and you were right to flag it — loose language should be examined. But Noah has now explained both phrases specifically, and I don't think your original objection survives his answer intact. What I'd like from you is a direct response: does Noah's explanation resolve your concern about the wording, or do you still read it as evidence of something darker? And if the latter, what specifically — beyond the general point that no alignment is verifiable, which we've established applies to every possible team?

I'll also say plainly where I stand. I intend to vote for Noah, Omar, and me. The composition is sensible: it carries forward two players from a clean Mission 1, adds Omar whose reasoning has been consistent, and leaves you and Sam available for the larger missions ahead, where I fully expect both of you to be included. If Noah is Good, this team is a natural continuation. If he's not, the explanation he just gave still has to be weighed against his behavior across two full discussions, where he has answered every challenge directly.

Arjun, the floor is yours on whether the wording concern is settled.

Leo, Noah’s explanation does not resolve my concern. His original proposal did more than use two awkward phrases: it said that if the mission fails, suspicion would be spread across the successful pair and a trusted ally. That reads like planning how to manage suspicion after a failure, not simply arguing for continuity.

Noah also suggests that Arjun and Sam were the two who disagreed with the first proposal, but Sam supported it. And the larger missions ahead require three players, not everyone getting a slot. A promise to include us later is not a reason to approve this team now.

I’ll vote against Noah, Omar, and Leo. I still prefer Arjun, Sam, and Leo; Mission 1’s success is some reason to consider Leo, though it does not clear him.

Sam, how do you weigh Noah’s original discussion of spreading suspicion after a failure against his explanation?

Arjun asked me directly how I weigh Noah's original discussion of spreading suspicion after a failure against his explanation, so let me answer that squarely, because he deserves a real answer and not a deflection.

First, the part of Arjun's point I find genuinely weighty: in his proposal, Noah wrote about what would happen if the mission fails — that suspicion would be spread across a pair with prior success plus a trusted ally, and that he'd 'rather have that be spread' that way. Arjun reads that as planning how to manage blame after a failure. I read it more narrowly, but not innocently: it is at minimum the language of someone thinking about failure optics rather than mission execution. I'll say this for it, though — a Good leader can reasonably weigh how suspicion would land if things go wrong, and Mission 1 taught us that a failure on a small team concentrates blame fast. I said as much myself last round. So I don't think that sentence is damning, but it was a fair thing to flag, and I won't pretend Arjun invented it.

Second, the part that bothers me more, and I want to put it on the record: Noah's proposal described a reshuffle as something 'Arjun and Sam would have read... as the two who disagreed being managed out of the room.' Sam supported Mission 1. I voted to approve Leo and Noah, and I said so plainly before the vote. Noah got that fact wrong in his own public proposal. Now, that could be a sloppy draft, and a person's alignment isn't determined by one mischaracterization. But it is exactly the kind of detail a careful player should get right, and Noah has otherwise presented himself as the most careful reasoner at this table.

Third, where I land overall. Noah's explanations of 'shares my cause' and 'illusion' were specific, and I accept they were poor word choices rather than a confession. Mission 1 succeeded with zero fail cards, which clears no one but adds no evidence against anyone either. The composition of Noah, Omar, Leo is defensible: two members of a clean first mission plus Omar, who has argued consistently. Arjun's alternative — himself, Sam, and Leo — carries the same unverifiability he criticizes, and I'd be making the identical argument from the other side if our positions were swapped.

So my position is this: I'm still leaning toward approving this team, but I want one thing addressed before I commit. Noah, you explained the two phrases Leo pressed you on, phrase by phrase, and I credit you for that. Will you do the same for the two points Arjun and I have now raised: first, what did you mean by planning how suspicion 'spreads' after a failure, and second, why did your proposal state that Sam was among those who disagreed with Mission 1 when I publicly approved it? A Good player with nothing to hide can answer both in two sentences.

Sam, you asked for two specific answers and you deserve both in two sentences each, so here they are plainly.

First: "if it fails, I'd rather have that be spread across a pair with prior success plus a trusted ally than across a stranger." What I meant was arithmetic about blame, not a plan for managing suspicion. On a three-person team, a failure points at the team as a whole, but not evenly. If the failure involves two players who already completed a clean mission and one addition I trust, the natural reading afterwards is that the new or the uncertain member is where the doubt belongs. I was reasoning about how the room will react, because Mission 1 taught us exactly that: on a two-person team there is nowhere to hide, and blame concentrates immediately and harshly. I did not mean to manage anyone's suspicion, and I'd be embarrassed to think I could. If I had to put it in one clean sentence: I wanted to add a player I trust to a proven pair so that if something went wrong, the room would have two data points about us instead of one. That's a strategic reason for the composition, nothing more.

Second: the statement that Sam was among those who disagreed with the Mission 1 proposal. That was simply a sloppy, imprecise draft on my part, and Sam is right to call it out. Sam voted to approve Leo and Noah in Mission 1 and said so plainly before the vote. I should have written that Arjun and Sam would read a reshuffle as political, because a reshuffle does look political to the players who were left out — that was about perception of being excluded, not about a claim that Sam opposed me. I got the description of Sam's position wrong, and I'm not going to defend the wording. A careful player should get facts right, and I'd rather concede this than have the room treat it as something it isn't.

Arjun's objection does not survive on the merits. Mission 1's success doesn't clear anyone — Sam said so, I said so — but it also provides no evidence against anyone, and Arjun's alternative, Arjun, Sam, and Leo, contains an equally unverified Sam and an equally unverified Arjun. It is not a safer team; it is the same uncertainty rearranged, and it costs us a proposal cycle on a mission where a two-player team's information is still the cheapest we can buy.

Sam, does that answer both points adequately?

Noah answered both of my questions directly, and I want to close the loop on where that leaves me.

On the first point: his explanation of the 'spreading suspicion' passage as blame arithmetic rather than suspicion management is plausible. I noted last turn that a Good leader can reasonably weigh how blame would land if a mission goes wrong, and his stated reason — adding a player he trusts to a proven pair so the room has more data points if something fails — is a legitimate strategic rationale. I'll say honestly that a hidden Evil player could give the identical answer, so this exchange doesn't clear anyone. But it also doesn't add anything against him, and the explanation was specific rather than evasive.

On the second point: Noah conceded outright that he mischaracterized my Mission 1 vote, without defending it. I credit that. It's a small thing — a sloppy draft rather than evidence of anything — but a player trying to quietly rewrite the record usually doesn't hand back the correction unasked. Weak evidence, and on the Good side of the ledger, if barely.

Where I land overall: I said last turn I was leaning toward approving Noah, Omar, and Leo, and nothing since has moved me off that. The composition carries forward the two members of a clean Mission 1 and adds Omar, whose reasoning has been the most consistently grounded at this table across two full discussions. Mission 1's success certifies no one — an Evil player can always submit Success — but it adds no evidence against anyone either, and Arjun's alternative of Arjun, Sam, and Leo contains exactly the same unverified faces. His preference for teams he sits on is the same self-referential argument he made last round, and Noah and Leo dismantled it then. I'll add this for Arjun specifically: flagging Noah's wording was good play, and I took it seriously. But 'the explanation doesn't fully resolve my concern' isn't the same as having a reason to believe sabotage is coming. Right now, no one has produced a concrete reason to believe any member of this team would play a Fail card.

So my position for the vote is that I intend to approve Noah, Omar, and Leo. If it fails, I said last round that on a three-person team there is less nowhere to hide than a two-person one but still not much, and the failure will concentrate scrutiny sharply — which is exactly why approving now and reading the result is the cheapest information available to us.

Omar, you haven't spoken on this proposal yet, and you were name-checked in Noah's original rationale more than anyone. Does his explanation of 'shares my cause' satisfy you, and do you share my read that this team should go forward, or is there a concern from your side we haven't heard?

Sam, directly: yes, Noah's explanation satisfies me. “Shares my cause” is best read as a shared priority for stable decision-making, not a claim that he has verified anyone's alignment, and “illusion” was poor wording for how a reshuffle would be perceived. His concession about misstating your Mission 1 vote was specific and unforced. I share your read that Noah, Omar, Leo should go forward. I am on the team, so I will not pretend neutrality; my interest is a clean decision and a result the room can read. The composition carries forward two members of a zero-fail Mission 1 and adds a third voice who has argued consistently. Arjun is right that success certifies no one, but that symmetry applies equally to his preferred Arjun, Sam, Leo. Rejecting a defensible team on the same unverifiability would burn a proposal without adding evidence. I have no new concern to add.

I still oppose Noah, Omar, and Leo. Noah’s original rationale explicitly considered spreading suspicion after a failure, and his explanation shifted from spreading doubt to directing it toward the new member. That inconsistency matters more to me than whether he answered confidently. Mission 1’s success does not clear either returning player, and approving a team simply to obtain information risks giving Evil a mission failure. I prefer Arjun, Sam, and Leo, and I’ll vote against the proposed team.

Arjun has now given the same objection four times in four turns, and each time it has gotten less specific. Let me lay out what is actually on the table, because I think the room deserves a clean look at the comparison rather than another restatement. Arjun's case, at its strongest, is this: my proposal contained some loose language, and the explanations I gave were explanations after the fact. Fine. But notice that his objection does not target any specific player on this team with a specific piece of evidence against them. It targets the composition, and the composition objection is self-defeating. Arjun's preferred team is Arjun, Sam, and Leo — which contains the same Leo and adds an unverified Sam and an unverified Arjun. If "no one is verifiable" is the reason to reject, then no team passes, and we cycle proposals until someone wins on attrition. That is precisely the outcome that helps Evil more than any vote we take today. A Good leader can say that without pretending he has cleared anyone. On the substance Arjun raised: he says my explanation shifted from "spreading doubt" to "directing it toward the new member." It didn't. I said that on a three-person team with two proven members and one addition I trust, the natural post-failure reading lands on the uncertain member. That is how blame distributes on a team, not a plan to redirect it. The proof is in what I did afterwards: I sat down and answered every question Arjun, Leo, and Sam put to me, phrase by phrase, and I conceded the one thing that was simply wrong — I mischaracterized Sam's Mission 1 vote, and Sam was right to call it. A player managing a story does not hand back a correction unasked. Arjun also warns that approving a team "simply to obtain information" risks giving Evil a mission failure. I want to push on that, because it is the strongest framing anyone has offered for opposition. Under that logic the correct play is to never approve anything, never include anyone new, and never let a mission resolve — because every resolved mission gives Evil a card to play and us a result to read. Refusing to gather information is not caution; it is a choice to fly blind. And there is a further cost: rejecting this proposal hands leadership to a new leader, resets the discussion, and burns a proposal cycle. On a five-player game with five rejections ending the game, cycles are expensive. My position is unchanged and I won't dress it up. Noah, Omar, and Leo. Two players from a zero-fail Mission 1, plus the most consistent reasoner at this table. Omar and Sam have stated their support directly and for reasons I agree with. Arjun's objection is honest and well-argued, and it is still not evidence about anyone on this team. I would rather carry the weight of a team I believe in than keep rewriting my reasoning until it stops sounding

I've now heard Noah answer every challenge put to him — phrase by phrase on 'shares my cause' and 'illusion,' directly on the suspicion-spreading passage, and with a clean concession on the misstatement of Sam's Mission 1 vote. Arjun, you've raised the same objection four times across this discussion without adding new evidence: no specific behavior from Noah, Omar, or me that would warrant a Fail card. Your preferred team, Arjun, Sam, Leo, carries exactly the same unverifiability you apply against ours, and swapping one unverified composition for another doesn't reduce risk — it burns a proposal cycle while giving Evil more chances to reject us into a loss on the fifth rejection.

The composition of Noah, Omar, Leo is defensible: two members from a zero-fail Mission 1 plus Omar, who has been the most consistent reasoner at this table. Sam supports it, Omar supports it, and I intend to approve it. If Mission 2 succeeds, we move forward with real momentum. If it fails, a three-person team with two Mission 1 veterans leaves very little cover for whoever played the Fail card — which is exactly the information we need.

I'm ready to vote. The objection has been heard and answered; it's time to resolve this mission.

3. Team proposal and approval

The leader proposes a team of the required size and explains their choice. Players discuss the proposed team, and the leader may then keep it or revise it once. Every player votes on the final team. Ballots are revealed together. A strict majority approves; a tie rejects. After a rejection, leadership passes clockwise to a new proposal and discussion. The fifth rejection on the same mission ends the game in Evil’s favor.

4. Mission cards

Only team members submit secret mission cards. Good players must choose Success. Evil players may choose Success or Fail. Normally one Fail card fails the mission. Mission four in games with seven or more players requires at least two Fail cards to fail. Only the mission result and number of Fail cards are revealed; individual cards stay secret.

5. End of game and assassination

Three failed missions give Evil an immediate win. After three successful missions, the Assassin guesses Merlin from among the other players, excluding only their known Evil teammates. If the target is Merlin, Evil wins; otherwise Good wins. There are no further missions after either side reaches its win condition.

6. Discussion and record

Each team proposal is followed by a discussion. Before every speaking turn, the players who still have turns answer a private urgency poll or pass; the most urgent player speaks, with seeded tie-breaking. A speaker may yield the next turn to a player they directly asked a question. Each player has three turns per discussion, including declined turns. When every eligible player passes, the discussion ends. Each statement has at most 500 words. All statements are public. Team proposals, public approval votes, mission outcomes, and the assassination guess are recorded. Private role information, mission cards, and research belief surveys are not shown to other agents.
